title: Dual Automatic Temperature Control (DATC): Component Locations
introduction:
The climate system has an air-moving team and a heat-moving team. The blower pushes cabin air, doors choose its route and temperature mix, and the refrigerant circuit carries heat outside. I use this DATC map to keep those jobs straight: asking the blower to fix every comfort complaint is rather like asking the kitchen fan to repair the fridge.

### Start at the dashboard

The dashboard drawing connects familiar outlets and controls to less obvious sensing locations. Follow the leader lines from the highlighted registers, the sunload sensor on top of the dashboard and the central control panel. FCIM means front controls interface module. The inset also identifies the in-vehicle temperature and humidity sensor in the lower instrument-panel area beside the steering column.

The registers are the outlets you feel air coming through. The cabin sensor and sunload sensor provide different information from the discharge-temperature sensors shown in the housing view. Sharing a dashboard does not make them interchangeable.

### Look inside the climate housing

The transparent housing view separates the blower motor from its speed control and places the door actuators around the air-handling assembly. I use the visible cylindrical blower fan as a landmark, then follow each leader line to the local table. The speed control adjusts the motor's electrical drive; the motor turns the fan.

The inlet door selects outside or recirculated air. The distribution door chooses the air's destination. Separate driver-side and passenger-side temperature door actuators belong to the dual-temperature arrangement. Those are different jobs, so the table's full component name matters. The temperature sensors identify particular sensing locations; the evaporator sensor monitors cooling at the evaporator and helps prevent icing.

### Follow the refrigerant hardware

The engine-bay view links the climate housing at the bulkhead to the compressor and the condenser at the front of the car. The thermostatic expansion valve meters refrigerant into the evaporator, while the receiver drier beside the condenser stores refrigerant and removes moisture inside the circuit. It is not a cabin-air filter.

Use each illustration with its own table: callouts restart between views. Follow the named line endpoints rather than treating the highlighting colors as a pressure chart. These drawings locate components; they do not provide connector access, pressure limits, charge quantities, fault verdicts or replacement instructions.

items.name: Recovery and charging equipment
items.detail: Refrigerant work requires the correct recovery and charging equipment and the matching service procedure. Identifying a line or fitting in this drawing is not an instruction to loosen it.

edits.text: NOTE: The 5.0L installation is shown; installations with all other engines are similar.
edits.why: Use the illustrations to recognize the component arrangement on DATC-equipped vehicles. Similarity across engines does not establish identical line routing, attachment details or service steps.
